description: The SELECT column list is missing commas between column names, causing a syntax error. Fix the query so it correctly retrieves id, username, and email from the users table.
broken_query: SELECT id username email FROM users;
gold_query: SELECT id, username, email FROM users;
hints: Check the column list in the SELECT statement.
SQL requires a comma separating each selected column.

description: The query joins users and orders but references 'id' without a table prefix. SQLite raises 'ambiguous column name: id' because both tables have an id column. Fix the query by qualifying the column with its table name so it returns each user's username alongside their order id.
broken_query: SELECT username, id FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
gold_query: SELECT users.username, orders.id FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
hints: When two tables share a column name, SQLite cannot tell which one you mean.
Prefix the ambiguous column with its table name, e.g. orders.id.
Both tables have an 'id' column — be explicit about which one you want.

description: This query is supposed to return delivered and shipped orders above a certain value but returns the wrong set of rows. Identify and fix the bug.
broken_query: SELECT id, user_id, status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' OR status = 'pending' AND total_amount > 500.00 ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
gold_query: SELECT id, user_id, status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE (status = 'cancelled' OR status = 'pending') AND total_amount > 500.00 ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

description: This query should return all orders from a specific date onwards but the row count does not match expectations. Fix it.
broken_query: SELECT id, user_id, status, total_amount, created_at FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) > '2025-02-15' ORDER BY created_at;
gold_query: SELECT id, user_id, status, total_amount, created_at FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) >= '2025-01-01' ORDER BY created_at;

description: This query returns correct results but becomes extremely slow as the products table grows. Fix the performance issue.
broken_query: SELECT id, name, (SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM order_items WHERE product_id = products.id) AS total_sold FROM products;
gold_query: SELECT products.id, products.name, COALESCE(SUM(order_items.quantity), 0) AS total_sold FROM products LEFT JOIN order_items ON products.id = order_items.product_id GROUP BY products.id, products.name;
hints: Consider how many times the database engine executes work for each row in the result.

description: This query ranks products by price but the rankings appear incorrect. Fix the query.
broken_query: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, c.name AS category, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY p.price DESC) AS price_rank FROM products p JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.id ORDER BY c.name, price_rank;
gold_query: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, c.name AS category, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id ORDER BY p.price DESC) AS price_rank FROM products p JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.id ORDER BY c.name, price_rank;
hints: The rankings look correct globally but may not reflect the intended grouping.

description: This query should return only users who have placed more than one order but it returns too many rows. Fix it.
broken_query: SELECT o.id AS order_id, u.username, COUNT(oi.id) AS item_count, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id GROUP BY o.id, u.username ORDER BY item_count DESC;
gold_query: SELECT o.id AS order_id, u.username, COUNT(oi.id) AS item_count, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id GROUP BY o.id, u.username HAVING COUNT(oi.id) > 1 ORDER BY item_count DESC;
hints: The query returns more rows than expected. Think about where result filtering should happen.

description: A 3-step reporting pipeline is producing wrong revenue figures. The pipeline calculates per-category revenue using CTEs. Each step depends on the previous. Fix all broken steps so the final result matches the expected output.
broken_query:
WITH
step1 AS (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) as total_qty
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY order_id
),
step2 AS (
    SELECT p.category_id, s.total_qty, p.price
    FROM products p
    JOIN step1 s ON p.id = s.product_id
),
step3 AS (
    SELECT category_id, SUM(total_qty) as units_sold, SUM(total_qty * price) as revenue
    FROM step2
    GROUP BY category_id
)
SELECT c.name as category, s.units_sold, s.revenue
FROM step3 s
JOIN categories c ON s.category_id = c.id
ORDER BY s.revenue DESC;
gold_query:
WITH
step1 AS (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) as total_qty
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY product_id
),
step2 AS (
    SELECT p.category_id, s.total_qty, p.price
    FROM products p
    JOIN step1 s ON p.id = s.product_id
),
step3 AS (
    SELECT category_id, SUM(total_qty) as units_sold, SUM(total_qty * price) as revenue
    FROM step2
    GROUP BY category_id
)
SELECT c.name as category, s.units_sold, s.revenue
FROM step3 s
JOIN categories c ON s.category_id = c.id
ORDER BY s.revenue DESC;
hints: Start by understanding what each step of the pipeline is supposed to produce before attempting any fix.
Run step1 in isolation first — does GROUP BY order_id make sense for computing per-product quantity totals?
The bug is in step1. Once step1 is wrong, every downstream step inherits the error.
